name: Moroccan Taktouka
imageAlt: Illustrative Moroccan grilled pepper salad; taktouka uses charred green peppers cooked with tomato
imageCredit: Photo: Ni4535, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. This is an illustrative Moroccan grilled pepper salad rather than a photograph of the exact green-pepper-and-tomato taktouka made on this page.
summary: Moroccan taktouka with charred green bell peppers folded into soft tomatoes, garlic, paprika, cumin and fresh herbs until the juices reduce to a smoky, scoopable cooked salad.
lead: Charred green peppers and tomatoes cook together with garlic and warm spices in a Moroccan salad made for scooping with bread.
about: Taktouka is a common Moroccan cooked salad or dip built principally from green bell peppers, tomatoes, garlic and olive oil. Moroccan cook and author Nargisse Benkabbou describes grilling the peppers until scorched and tender, then simmering them with softened tomatoes, herbs, paprika and cumin until the liquid evaporates. It can be served warm or cold, with bread, beside grilled foods or in a sandwich.
story: Moroccan tables often present several salads and vegetable preparations at once, and taktouka belongs to that family of small dishes rather than to the Western idea of a raw leafy salad. Its defining contrast is smoke and sweetness: the peppers are charred before they meet tomatoes that have cooked down until concentrated. It is related in serving role to zaalouk, but the two should stay distinct - taktouka centers peppers and tomato, while zaalouk centers eggplant and tomato. Household versions vary in pepper color, chile heat, tomato sweetness and how finely the vegetables are chopped.
caveat: This recipe follows a charred-green-pepper Moroccan home style. Some cooks leave taktouka chunkier or softer, and tomato sweetness varies enough that a pinch of sugar is sometimes used; add it only if the finished tomatoes are noticeably sharp, not by default.
prepNotes: The peppers should be blackened in patches over most of the skin and feel limp, not merely browned on one face.
Let the hot peppers rest under a bowl or in a covered container for about 10 minutes; trapped steam loosens the skins without rinsing away smoky flavor.
Taktouka should be moist but not soupy. The final simmer is finished when a spoon moved across the pan does not immediately fill with watery tomato juice.
ingredients: 3 large green bell peppers
4 large ripe tomatoes, peeled, seeded and roughly chopped
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 garlic cloves, finely chopped
2 tbsp chopped fresh cilantro
2 tbsp chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 tsp sweet paprika
1/2 tsp ground cumin
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Pinch cayenne, optional
Pinch sugar only if the tomatoes are sharply acidic, optional
steps: Heat a broiler, outdoor grill or grill pan to high. Char the whole green peppers, turning every 3 to 4 minutes, until all sides are blistered and blackened in patches and the flesh feels soft, about 12 to 16 minutes total.

Transfer the hot peppers to a bowl and cover for 10 minutes. Checkpoint: when uncovered, the skins should wrinkle and slip away easily; the peppers should smell smoky and sweet rather than raw and grassy.
Peel the peppers without rinsing them, remove stems and seeds, and cut the flesh into roughly 1-inch pieces.

Warm the olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add the tomatoes, garlic, cilantro, parsley, paprika, cumin, salt, optional cayenne and optional sugar. Cover and cook 10 minutes, stirring twice, until the tomatoes collapse and release their juice.

Uncover and cook 5 to 8 minutes more, stirring often. Checkpoint: the raw tomato smell should be gone, the garlic should smell mellow rather than sharp, and the tomato mixture should look thick enough to coat the spoon.

Fold in the charred green peppers and simmer gently, uncovered, for about 10 minutes. Stir and lightly press some of the vegetables with the spoon, keeping visible pieces rather than pureeing the salad.

Checkpoint: almost all free liquid should have evaporated, the peppers should be completely tender, and the mixture should hold together in a soft mound when pushed to one side of the pan. If water pools around it, continue simmering a few minutes.
Taste for salt, cumin and heat. Serve warm or at room temperature with Moroccan bread or other crusty bread, or alongside grilled meat or fish.
sources: My Moroccan Food - Taktouka by Moroccan cook and author Nargisse Benkabbou

name: Puerto Rican Arroz con Gandules
imageAlt: Puerto Rican arroz con gandules with rice and pigeon peas
imageCredit: Photo: Jose Kevo, Wikimedia Commons/Flickr, CC BY-SA 2.0
summary: Puerto Rican arroz con gandules with medium-grain rice, pigeon peas, sofrito, smoked ham, achiote and alcaparrado cooked together in a caldero until the grains are tender and fragrant.
lead: Sofrito, achiote, pigeon peas and rice share one pot in a Puerto Rican staple that is especially inseparable from the Christmas table.
about: Discover Puerto Rico identifies arroz con gandules as Puerto Rico's national dish and a centerpiece of the Christmas table. Its published recipe from chefs Itza Robles and Efren Robles combines medium-grain rice, green pigeon peas, achiote oil, ham, sofrito, alcaparrado and sazón before the rice finishes covered over low heat. The dish is eaten year-round, and Puerto Rican chef Wilo Benet notes that households have their own variations.
story: Arroz con gandules is a one-pot rice dish whose Puerto Rican identity comes from more than pigeon peas alone. Sofrito supplies the aromatic base, achiote colors and perfumes the fat, and olives and capers add the briny note associated with many island rice preparations. Pork is common but quantities and forms vary, and some families use banana or plantain leaves to help hold steam over the rice. Holiday service beside pernil is iconic, but the dish is not limited to December.
caveat: Puerto Rican households vary in sofrito, pork, olives, capers, sazón and cooking liquid. This version follows the structure published by Discover Puerto Rico while keeping cumin optional and treating sazón as part of the seasoning system rather than a universal requirement for every family pot.
prepNotes: It gives the tender, cohesive-but-separate texture used in the Discover Puerto Rico recipe. Rinse briefly and drain well so added water stays predictable.
Taste the liquid before the rice
Ham, alcaparrado, sazón and canned gandules can all contribute salt. Adjust the broth before the rice absorbs it.
After the liquid drops below the rice surface, lower the heat, cover and leave the grains largely undisturbed so they steam instead of breaking down.
ingredients: 3 cups medium-grain white rice, rinsed briefly and drained well
1 can (15 oz) green pigeon peas (gandules), with their liquid
4 tbsp achiote or annatto oil
1/2 lb cooked or smoked ham, cut into small dice
1/2 cup Puerto Rican sofrito made with onion, garlic, sweet peppers, cilantro and culantro
2 tbsp alcaparrado, drained and chopped if the olives are large
1 packet sazón con achiote, optional according to household preference
1 tsp dried oregano
1 tsp ground cumin, optional
1 bay leaf
3 1/2 cups low-sodium chicken broth or water
Kosher salt, only as needed after tasting the cooking liquid
steps: Heat the achiote oil in a caldero or heavy 5- to 6-quart pot over medium heat. Add the diced ham and cook 4 to 6 minutes, stirring, until the edges take on light golden color and smell savory rather than raw.

Add the sofrito, alcaparrado, bay leaf, optional sazón, oregano and optional cumin. Cook 3 to 5 minutes, stirring often. Checkpoint: the sofrito should darken slightly and smell sweet and aromatic, with no raw onion or pepper aroma remaining.

Stir in the gandules with their liquid, then add the broth or water. Bring to a lively simmer and taste the liquid; add salt only if needed because the ham, olives, capers and sazón may already provide enough.
Stir in the drained rice and bring back to a steady boil over medium heat. Cook uncovered 10 to 15 minutes, stirring only once or twice near the beginning so the rice distributes evenly.

Checkpoint: the liquid should fall to roughly the level of the rice, the surface grains should become visible with small bubbles breaking between them, and the aroma should be strongly of sofrito and achiote rather than raw starch.
Lower the heat to the lowest setting, gently turn the rice once from the outer edge toward the center, cover tightly and cook 25 to 30 minutes without repeatedly opening the lid.

Open the pot and test grains from the center. Checkpoint: the rice should be tender all the way through, the gandules should remain intact, and no wet broth should pool at the bottom. If the center is still firm, sprinkle in 2 to 3 tablespoons hot water, cover and steam 5 minutes more.

Fluff gently with a fork or broad spoon, cover again and rest off the heat for 8 to 10 minutes. Serve hot with pernil, roast pork or other Puerto Rican mains, or as a substantial rice dish on its own.
sources: Discover Puerto Rico - Traditional Puerto Rican Arroz con Gandules by chefs Itza Robles and Efren Robles

name: Georgian Chakapuli
imageAlt: Georgian chakapuli lamb and green herb stew
imageCredit: Photo: Georgian Recipes / Georgia About, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0; attribution required to GeorgianRecipes.net
summary: Georgian chakapuli with lamb, an abundance of fresh tarragon and herbs, sorrel, green tkemali and dry white wine simmered gently into a tart, intensely spring-green stew.
lead: Lamb cooks under armfuls of spring herbs, tart plum sauce and white wine in chakapuli, a Georgian stew closely associated with Easter and the green season.
about: Georgia's national tourism authority describes chakapuli as a symbolic spring and Easter dish built from tender lamb, fresh herbs, sorrel, green onion, green pepper, tarragon, tkemali plum and white wine. The official method layers meat and herbs, adds wine immediately, brings in tkemali before the lamb is fully tender and cooks everything gently so the sour plum, wine and herbs form one bright sauce.
story: Chakapuli is a dish in which seasonality is visible in the pot. Georgia Travel emphasizes tarragon, sorrel and other spring greens and links the stew strongly with Easter. It also documents meaningful variation: veal can replace lamb, and contemporary versions may use chicken, fish, mushrooms, eggs or potatoes. The traditional lamb form remains distinctive because fatty meat, sharp tkemali and large quantities of fresh herbs balance one another. Kakhetian qvevri white wine is singled out by the tourism authority, reflecting the dish's connection to Georgia's wine culture as well as its spring table.
caveat: This is a scaled home version of the lamb preparation documented by Georgia Travel. A dry Georgian white wine is ideal; another dry, unoaked white wine is a practical cooking substitute but not culturally identical. Fresh tarragon and tkemali are defining flavors and should not be replaced with dried tarragon or ordinary sweet plum jam.
prepNotes: Buy much more herbs than seems normal
Chakapuli is not a meat stew garnished with herbs. The herbs collapse into the cooking liquid and are a major part of the dish's body and aroma.
Use tender tips and leaves; thick woody stems stay stringy even after simmering.
Hard boiling drives off wine aroma quickly and can tighten the lamb before its connective tissue softens. Aim for lazy bubbles, not a rolling boil.
ingredients: 2 1/4 lb lamb shoulder or neck, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces, preferably with some fat
1 medium yellow onion, thinly sliced
8 green onions, sliced into 1-inch pieces
4 packed cups fresh tarragon leaves and tender tips
2 packed cups fresh sorrel, roughly chopped
2 packed cups fresh cilantro, roughly chopped
1 packed cup flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
1/2 cup fresh mint leaves, roughly torn
1 to 2 fresh green chiles, slit or sliced to taste
1 1/2 cups dry Georgian white wine or another dry unoaked white wine
1 cup green tkemali plum sauce
1 1/4 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Freshly ground black pepper to taste
steps: Pat the lamb dry. If it has a few very fatty trimmings, finely chop about 2 tablespoons of them and place them in a heavy Dutch oven over medium-low heat. Cook 4 to 6 minutes until some fat renders; remove any hard browned solids. If your lamb is lean, begin with 1 tablespoon neutral oil instead.

Spread half the sliced onion and green onions over the bottom, add the lamb, then cover with about two-thirds of the tarragon, sorrel, cilantro, parsley and mint. Add the green chile and pour the wine around the meat.

Bring the pot just to a simmer over medium heat, then immediately reduce to low, cover and cook 25 minutes. Checkpoint: the herbs should collapse dramatically, the pot should smell strongly of tarragon and wine, and the liquid should show only lazy bubbles rather than a hard boil.
Add the green tkemali and gently turn the meat and herbs together. Cover partially and continue cooking 35 to 50 minutes, stirring only occasionally so the lamb pieces stay intact.

Checkpoint: the lamb is ready when a fork slides into a piece with little resistance and the connective tissue feels tender rather than rubbery. The sauce should taste distinctly tart and herbaceous, with the alcohol's harsh edge cooked away.
Add the remaining onion, green onion and reserved fresh herbs during the final 5 minutes so the stew regains a fresh green aroma and layered texture. Season with salt and black pepper.

If the pot is very watery after the lamb is tender, uncover and simmer gently 5 to 10 minutes. Do not reduce until thick or brown; chakapuli should retain a loose green-tinted broth around the meat and herbs.
Rest off the heat for 10 minutes, then taste again for salt and tkemali acidity. Serve hot with Georgian bread or another sturdy bread for the broth.
sources: Georgia Travel - Chakapuli: traditional ingredients, technique and Easter context
